areas.name: Patients
areas.detail: Who the person is, what they live with, and the plan for their care

areas.name: Clinical
areas.detail: What was found, decided, prescribed, tested and referred

areas.name: Care network
areas.detail: The people and places authorised to deliver that care

areas.name: Operations
areas.detail: Getting the right person to the right place at the right time

areas.name: Finance
areas.detail: What was charged, claimed, authorised and paid

areas.name: Governance
areas.detail: Who agreed to what, and who looked at it afterwards

sensitivity.name: Routine
sensitivity.detail: Administrative. Carries no clinical finding on its own.

sensitivity.name: Clinical
sensitivity.detail: Health information, and therefore special personal information under POPIA section 26.

sensitivity.name: Protected
sensitivity.detail: Clinical, and carrying a risk of harm on disclosure beyond the record itself: sexual and reproductive health, mental health, HIV, substance use, termination of pregnancy and gender-affirming care.
sensitivity.summaryHeader: never — the header says a category is withheld rather than omitting it silently
sensitivity.note: The list is held here rather than parsed out of the sentence above, so a category added to the contract is withheld everywhere without anyone editing a screen.

records.name: Patient
records.summary: Identity, contact, preferred facility and next of kin.

records.name: Household
records.summary: The people who live and are cared for together. Membership is not consent: each member's record stays their own.

records.name: Allergies
records.summary: Medicine, food and environmental allergies with severity. Carried in the summary because a dispensing pharmacist needs it before anything else.

records.name: Vitals
records.summary: Blood pressure, pulse, temperature, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, weight, BMI and glucose, as a series rather than a last reading.

records.name: Chronic conditions
records.summary: Long-term conditions with status and who manages them. HIV and mental-health conditions are protected and are held separately.

records.name: Diagnoses
records.summary: Diagnoses with onset, status and the clinician accountable for each.

records.name: Medical history
records.summary: Previous illnesses, operations, admissions, family and social history.

records.name: Immunisations
records.summary: Vaccines given, batch, site and what is due next.

records.name: Maternal health
records.summary: Pregnancy, antenatal visits, scans, risk factors, delivery and postnatal care. Protected because it includes outcomes a person may never have disclosed at home.

records.name: Child health
records.summary: Growth, milestones and paediatric history. A child's protected categories are the child's, not the guardian's.

records.name: Care plan
records.summary: Goals, activities, the provider responsible for each and progress against them.

records.name: Emergency card
records.summary: Blood group, allergies, critical conditions, current medicine and one contact. The smallest set that helps a stranger in an emergency, and nothing more.

records.name: Consultations
records.summary: Every encounter in one structure, so two clinicians do not record the same visit in two shapes.

records.name: Procedures
records.summary: What was done, when, by whom, with outcome and complications.

records.name: Prescriptions
records.summary: Medicine, dose, frequency, repeats and the prescribing clinician's registration. A pharmacy opens this on its dispensing licence: vetting.json promises it sees the prescription and the allergies that bear on filling it, and a Medication tab that opens on nothing was that promise unkept.

records.name: Medicine catalogue
records.summary: Generic name, brand, strength, form, schedule and warnings. A formulary, not patient information.

records.name: Dispensing
records.summary: What was actually handed over, by which pharmacy, and what is outstanding.

records.name: Laboratory
records.summary: Tests requested, specimen and chain of custody, results with reference ranges, and release as a deliberate clinical act.

records.name: Imaging
records.summary: X-ray, ultrasound, CT and MRI with the reporting radiologist.

records.name: Referrals
records.summary: Who to, why, how urgently, and what came back. Reading a referral and making one are different acts: a nurse who may not refer still has to know their patient was referred.

records.name: Admissions
records.summary: Admission, ward, treating doctor, procedures, discharge summary and follow-up.

records.name: Providers
records.summary: A practitioner and the roles they hold. Their right to practise is the vetting record, not a field here.

records.name: Facilities
records.summary: Clinic, hospital, pharmacy, laboratory or imaging centre, and what it is accredited for.

records.name: Caregivers
records.summary: A family or home-based carer linked to the patient, with the authority they actually hold.

records.name: Care team
records.summary: Everyone currently authorised for this patient, and since when.

records.name: Vetting evidence
records.summary: A registration certificate, a police clearance, a schedule of cover — the document a reviewer actually looked at, sealed, versioned, and hashed so a substitution shows. Routine by this catalogue's own definition: a police clearance carries no clinical finding. Marking it clinical to buy a higher ceiling would drag it into reach of the treatment and dispensing purposes, which have no business with it; what keeps it narrow is review-vetting, held by one role in the whole catalogue.

records.name: Appointments
records.summary: Booked, attended, missed and cancelled, with the reason recorded rather than inferred.

records.name: Home visits
records.summary: The visit itself: who attended, what was observed, what was escalated.

records.name: Tasks
records.summary: Work assigned to a named person with a due time, not a shared list nobody owns.

records.name: Case management
records.summary: A long-running case coordinated across several providers.

records.name: Patient transport
records.summary: Getting a patient to care, and the handover at each end.

records.name: Medicine collection
records.summary: Chronic medicine ready, collected, or missed — the point at which adherence is actually observable.

records.name: Community health
records.summary: Work by community health workers and at Thuso Corner sites.

records.name: Social support
records.summary: Links to social workers, NGOs, shelters and government grants. Protected because it can disclose abuse, homelessness or destitution.

records.name: Medical aid
records.summary: Scheme, plan, membership and dependant code.

records.name: Claims
records.summary: Submitted, accepted or rejected, with the reason. Carries the service code, never the diagnosis in words.

records.name: Authorisations
records.summary: Pre-authorisation, what it covers and when it lapses.

records.name: Invoices
records.summary: Services rendered, tariff, VAT and the patient's portion.

records.name: Payments
records.summary: Card, EFT, wallet or scheme payment against an invoice.

records.name: Consent
records.summary: What was agreed, in which words, on what date — and withdrawal, which is a first-class event rather than a deletion.

records.name: Access grants
records.summary: Who may see this record, which part, until when, and who granted it.

records.name: Documents
records.summary: Identity, scheme card, consent forms, referral letters, certificates and reports.

records.name: Audit
records.summary: Who opened, changed, exported or shared a record, and when. Append-only, and readable by the patient.

consultation.why: One shape for every encounter, because a record two clinicians write two ways is a record neither can safely read. The sections are the same whether a nurse or a doctor is writing; what differs is what each is allowed to conclude.

sections.name: Symptoms and history of present illness
Observations and vitals
sections.note: Reference ranges are indicative and are not a validated early-warning score.

sections.name: Assessment
sections.note: A nurse records an assessment. A diagnosis is a doctor's, and the form says so rather than relying on training.

sections.name: Clinician and registration
sections.note: Name, council registration and the moment of signing. Attribution is not a footer.

soap.name: Subjective
soap.detail: What the patient reports, in their words where it matters.

soap.name: Assessment
soap.detail: The clinical assessment, or the diagnosis where the writer may make one.

soap.name: Plan
soap.detail: Treatment, medicine, tests, referral and follow-up.

observations.why: The seven readings a nurse takes at the door, and the indicative adult range each is flagged against. They lived in a React component, which meant a number that decides whether a reading is put in front of a doctor was declared on a screen and two native apps were checked against that screen. A reference range is contract, not presentation. The sentence that qualifies it is not repeated here: it is the note on the “observations” consultation section above, and every platform renders that one.

explanations.why: What each of the seven readings measures, what a number outside its range may follow from, and what a person can do about it today. This is the paragraph the Health Passport never had: a number beside a range answers “is this inside the lines” and not the question somebody opened the screen with, which is “should I be worried”. Left unanswered, that question is asked of a search engine, and a search engine will diagnose them. It sits here, beside the observations section whose note already calls those ranges indicative, because it was written three times — once in apps/web/src/lib/explain.ts, once in apps/ios/MyThuso/Models/Explain.swift and once in apps/android/app/src/main/java/za/co/mythuso/model/Explain.kt — with nothing comparing the copies. Every agent that typed the second or third copy said in a comment that it belonged here. This is here.
explanations.whyProseAndNotAModel: “screening” is one of the capabilities in packages/catalog/capabilities.json and it is blocked on a model, a vendor and a licence. It is also the easiest thing in this product to overstate. A written explanation cannot be any of the things an unlicensed model would be: it cannot see your record, it cannot personalise itself, it cannot be confidently wrong in a new way for each reader, and it can be read in full by a clinician before it ships. When screening arrives it will have to be better than this, and this is what “better” will be measured against.
explanations.theLineItMustNotCross: Nothing here diagnoses. Each entry says what the measurement is, what a number outside the range *may* follow from — the ordinary, boring causes first, because they are usually the right ones — and what to do, which is nearly always “have it taken again” and never “start, stop or change a medicine”. Every entry ends at the same place: a registered doctor decides what a reading means for a particular person, and a screen does not.
explanations.whatIsNotHere: No label, no unit and no reference range. Those are the observations section above, and a copy of one beside the prose that explains it would be the fourth place a number that decides whether a doctor sees something is written down. The urgent conditions are ids into packages/catalog/sos.json — the red flags that end the questions and show the ambulance number — so a screen can neither invent one nor soften one, and a check fails the build if an id here is not a red flag there.

entries.measures: The push of blood against your artery walls at the moment your heart squeezes. It is the first and larger of the two numbers in a blood-pressure reading.
entries.above: A single high reading is common and is not high blood pressure on its own. Walking to the door, coffee, a cigarette, pain, a full bladder, a cuff that is too small for the arm or a dose taken late will all lift it. It can also be the first sign of high blood pressure, which is why the answer to one high reading is another reading rather than a decision.
entries.below: A low systolic is often just how somebody is built, and is common in people who are young, fit or well hydrated. It is worth attention when it arrives with dizziness on standing, fainting, a racing heart or confusion.
entries.whatToDo: Sit still for five minutes with your back supported and both feet on the floor, then have it taken again on the same arm. Keep the boxes of everything you take and show them to the nurse at the next visit — the commonest reason a reading moves is a dose that was missed, doubled or changed by somebody else.

entries.measures: The pressure still in your arteries between beats, while the heart is refilling. It is the second and smaller of the two numbers.
entries.above: It tends to move with the first number and follows the same everyday things. On its own, one raised diastolic reading means the reading should be repeated, not that anything has been found.
entries.below: Usually unremarkable, and often lower in people who are fit. It matters alongside symptoms — light-headedness when you stand, or feeling faint — rather than by itself.
entries.whatToDo: It is taken in the same measurement as the first number, so the same thing applies: sit quietly, have it repeated, and bring your medicines to the visit so the nurse can see what you are actually taking.

entries.measures: How many times your heart beats in a minute, counted while you are resting.
entries.above: A fast resting pulse follows exertion, anxiety, pain, fever, dehydration, caffeine, some inhalers and some cold remedies. It settles as the cause does. A pulse that stays fast at rest, or that is irregular, is something a doctor should look at rather than something to watch alone.
entries.below: A slow pulse is normal in people who are fit, and is expected with some heart and blood-pressure medicines. It is worth reporting if it comes with feeling faint, unusually tired or short of breath.
entries.whatToDo: Sit for five minutes and have it counted again. If it is often irregular, say so at the next visit — the pattern over several visits tells a doctor far more than any single count.

entries.measures: How many breaths you take in a minute, counted while you are sitting quietly and, ideally, not thinking about it.
entries.above: Breathing faster follows exercise, fever, pain, anxiety and a chest infection. It is one of the earliest things to change when somebody is becoming unwell, which is why a nurse counts it even when you feel fine.
entries.below: Slow breathing at rest is usually nothing. It matters when somebody is unusually drowsy or difficult to wake, particularly if they are taking strong pain medicine.
entries.whatToDo: If you are breathing faster than usual and it is not settling, book a visit rather than waiting for the next one. Bring the inhalers or chest medicines you use, if you use any.

entries.measures: How warm your body is, taken with the same thermometer in the same place each time so that two visits can be compared.
entries.above: A raised temperature is the body responding to something, most often an infection it will deal with. Where it was taken changes the number — under the arm reads lower than in the ear — so the place it was taken matters as much as the figure.
entries.below: A low reading is often the thermometer, the room or a cold hand rather than the person. In an older adult, a genuinely low temperature alongside feeling unwell deserves the same attention a fever would.
entries.whatToDo: Drink water, rest, and take it again in a few hours. A fever that lasts more than a couple of days, or one in a baby, is a reason to book a visit or see a doctor rather than to keep measuring.

entries.measures: The share of your blood that is carrying oxygen, read through a fingertip by a clip that shines light through it.
entries.above: There is no reading above this range to explain: the scale stops at a hundred.
entries.below: A low reading is often the device rather than the person — cold hands, poor circulation, nail varnish, false nails, movement, or a finger that is not in it properly. It is worth knowing that these clips are less accurate on darker skin and have been found to read higher than the truth, so a borderline reading on a person who feels short of breath should be believed less than the person is.
entries.whatToDo: Warm your hand, take off any nail varnish, sit still and try again on a different finger. If it stays low, or if you are breathless doing something you managed easily last week, book a visit.

entries.measures: How much sugar is in your blood at the moment it was taken, from a drop of blood on a strip.
entries.above: When you last ate changes this reading more than almost anything else, so a number taken after a meal is not the same measurement as one taken fasting, and the range here is the fasting one. A high reading is a reason to have it repeated properly, and repeatedly high readings are how diabetes is found — by a doctor, on more than one occasion, not on one strip.
entries.below: A low reading matters sooner than a high one. It can follow a missed meal, alcohol, unusual exercise, or diabetes medicine taken without food. Shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion or irritability alongside a low reading is the body asking for sugar now.
entries.whatToDo: If it is low and you feel it, eat or drink something sugary and then something more substantial, and tell the nurse or a doctor that it happened. If it is high, note when you last ate and have it taken again fasting. Never change the dose of a diabetes medicine on the strength of a reading at home.

explanations.provenanceWhy: Where this text comes from and what it is not. Five sentences that have to be on the screen rather than in a policy: a reader deciding how much weight to give a paragraph about their own blood pressure is owed the provenance of it before the paragraph, not after. Two of them are the ones a generator must never be allowed to quietly retire — the text is written, not produced by software, and no clinician has reviewed the wording. Generating the prose into Swift and Kotlin does not make it reviewed, and the day it is reviewed somebody has to change the sentence rather than let a build do it for them.

provenance.written: Everything on this screen is written text held inside the app. Everybody sees the same words for the same reading, nothing here has read your record in order to write them, and no software has looked at your numbers and formed a view.
provenance.unreviewed: No clinician has reviewed this wording yet. It is written down rather than left unsaid so that a doctor can correct it — a paragraph somebody can argue with is worth more than a screen that explains nothing at all.
provenance.ranges: The ranges are the indicative adult ranges the nurse’s own assessment is held to. They are a guide for a healthy adult, not a validated early-warning score, and your own doctor may work to different numbers for you.
provenance.whoDecides: None of this is a diagnosis and none of it is advice about your treatment. A reading is one measurement, on one day, in one room. What it means for you is a clinical judgement, and it is made by the registered doctor who reviews your record.
provenance.neverChange: Nothing here is a reason to start, stop or change a medicine. That decision belongs to whoever prescribed it.

summaryCard.why: The page a stranger reads when there is no time to read the file. It is deliberately small: every field earns its place by changing what someone would do in the next ten minutes.
summaryCard.withheld: Protected categories never appear. The card says a category is withheld rather than omitting it silently, so a clinician knows to ask rather than assuming there is nothing to know.
